**Title:** The Leak That Unmasked the Magic: How a Leaked Video Exposed Tom Cruise and Scientology to the World

In January 2008, the nascent video-sharing platform YouTube and the tabloid blog *Gawker* became the battleground for one of the early digital era’s most defining clashes between institutional secretiveness and internet freedom. At the center of the storm was a nine-minute, internal promotional video featuring Hollywood’s biggest movie star, Tom Cruise. Filmed in 2004, the video was never intended for non-Scientologist eyes. However, its sudden, unauthorized release provided the global public with an unprecedented, highly bizarre look into the inner workings of the Church of Scientology—and severely dented the carefully managed image of its most famous adherent.

### Behind Closed Doors: The 2004 Video

The video was originally produced for an internal Scientology event in 2004, during which Cruise was awarded the church’s newly minted "Freedom Medal of Valor" by its leader, David Miscavige. Set to a score that featured music from Cruise’s *Mission: Impossible* franchise, the interview-style feature showed the actor dressed in a dark suit, speaking directly to the camera with intense, boundary-pushing enthusiasm. 

For the average viewer, Cruise’s monologue was nearly unintelligible, filled with insular church jargon. He spoke fervently about "KSW" (Keeping Scientology Working), "SPs" (Suppressive Persons), and the heavy responsibility of being a Scientologist. "When you're a Scientologist, and you drive by an accident, it's not like anyone else," Cruise declared in the video. "As you drive by, you know you have to do something about it, because you're the only one who can really help."

The footage reached its climax with footage of Cruise exchanging formal, military-style salutes with portraits of Scientology founder L. Ron Hubbard and church leader David Miscavige. Coupled with Cruise’s sudden bursts of manic laughter and unblinking intensity, the video appeared less like a celebrity endorsement and more like an unvarnished glimpse into a high-stakes, highly disciplined hierarchy.

### The Leak and the Legal War

When the video leaked online four years after its creation, it spread like wildfire. The Church of Scientology, notorious for its aggressive legal tactics and strict control over its intellectual property, acted swiftly. Their legal team issued a flurry of cease-and-desist letters and Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) takedown notices, claiming copyright infringement. 

YouTube complied with the legal threats, removing the video from its site. However, *Gawker* refused to back down. Editor Nick Denton argued that the video was a matter of legitimate public interest, publishing it under the defense of fair use. *Gawker*’s stance invited a massive surge in traffic, as millions flocked to the site to see the footage the Church was desperately trying to scrub from the internet.

Instead of hiding the video, the Church’s heavy-handed attempts at censorship triggered a classic case of the "Streisand Effect"—where the effort to suppress information directly causes it to become vastly more famous.

### The Birth of "Project Chanology"

The attempt to censor the internet sparked an unprecedented backlash. The loosely organized online collective known as "Anonymous" took up the video as a rallying cry against digital censorship. Declaring war on Scientology, Anonymous launched "Project Chanology," a campaign that combined cyberattacks (like Distributed Denial of Service attacks on church websites) with real-world, peaceful protests outside Scientology centers globally. 

Thousands of masked protesters wearing Guy Fawkes masks appeared outside Scientology chanteries in cities like Los Angeles, London, and Sydney. The Cruise video had unwittingly transformed Anonymous from an obscure internet subculture into a visible, global activist movement.

### A Watershed Moment for Tom Cruise and Scientology

For Tom Cruise, the leak came at a particularly vulnerable time. It followed a string of public relations missteps in 2005, including his infamous couch-jumping incident on *The Oprah Winfrey Show* and an aggressive interview with Matt Lauer on *Today* regarding psychiatry. The 2004 video reinforced the growing public perception that Cruise was detached from reality and deeply entrenched in a secretive organization. 

Prior to the leak, the Church of Scientology had managed to maintain a polished, enigmatic public image, largely obscured behind celebrity spokespeople and expensive real estate. The leaked video stripped away that veneer. It showed the world the internal, radicalized culture of the organization—a culture that demanded total devotion, military-style discipline, and an "us versus them" mentality toward the rest of society.

Ultimately, the 2008 leak proved to be a turning point. It marked the moment Scientology lost its battle to control its own public narrative in the age of the open web, and it forced Tom Cruise to dramatically retreat from discussing his religious beliefs publicly, retreating back to the safer territory of pure blockbuster cinema.

**(CNN)** -- A surreal, nine-minute internal promotional video featuring Hollywood superstar Tom Cruise passionately extolling the virtues of Scientology has leaked online, setting off a high-stakes legal battle and a frenzy across the blogosphere.

The video, filmed in 2004 but published online this week, depicts the 45-year-old *Mission: Impossible* actor wearing a black turtleneck and speaking intensely about his devotion to the Church of Scientology, punctuated by dramatic laughter and set to the theme music of his hit movie franchises. 

"Being a Scientologist, when you drive past an accident, it’s not like anyone else," Cruise says in the video. "As you drive past, you know you have to do something about it, because you’re the only one who can really help."

He adds later in the clip: "We are the authorities on getting people off drugs. We are the authorities on the mind. We are the authorities on improving conditions... We can rehabilitate criminals."

The video was originally produced for a 2004 Scientology gala in which Cruise was awarded the church's International Association of Scientologists (IAS) Freedom Medal of Valor. However, its sudden appearance on video-sharing sites YouTube and Google Video has drawn sharp legal fire from church leadership.

### Gawker refuses to pull video

Attorneys for the Church of Scientology quickly issued cease-and-desist letters to several Web sites hosting the footage, alleging copyright infringement. While YouTube removed several copies of the video, New York-based media blog Gawker refused to back down. 

Gawker published the video in its entirety on its flagship site and its Hollywood sub-blog, Defamer, arguing that the footage is newsworthy and protected under "fair use" legal doctrines. 

"It's newsworthy, and we're not taking it down," Gawker editor Nick Denton said in a statement on the site. Gawker executives argued that the video provides public insight into one of the world's most high-profile actors and his relationship with the controversial organization.

Internet rights groups and online activists have also stepped in, mirroring the video across dozens of international servers to prevent the church from erasing it from the web entirely. 

### Book paints dramatic picture of Cruise's influence

The video's leak comes at a deeply inconvenient time for Cruise and his public relations team, arriving the very same week as the release of a highly anticipated, unauthorized biography by British journalist Andrew Morton.

Morton, famous for his explosive 1992 biography *Diana: Her True Story*, turns his lens on the actor in *Tom Cruise: An Unauthorized Biography*, which hit bookstore shelves on Tuesday. 

In the book, Morton claims that Cruise has risen to become the effective "second-in-command" of the Church of Scientology, wielding immense influence over its leader, David Miscavige. The biography also alleges that Scientology leaders played a direct role in ending Cruise’s marriage to actress Nicole Kidman and vetting his current wife, Katie Holmes.

Representatives for both Cruise and the Church of Scientology have fiercely denied the claims in Morton's book. 

In a statement released Tuesday, church officials called the book "a malicious mixture of long-debunked myths, scuttlebutt and outright lies." Cruise's attorney, Bert Fields, characterized the biography as "scurrilous" and "boring," threatening legal action against Morton and publisher St. Martin's Press.

### A pattern of PR headaches

For Cruise, the twin crises of the leaked video and Morton’s biography mark the latest chapter in a turbulent few years for his public image. 

Once considered Hollywood’s most bankable and controlled star, Cruise’s public standing took a hit in 2005 following an erratic appearance on *The Oprah Winfrey Show*—where he jumped on a couch to declare his love for Holmes—and a tense interview on NBC’s *Today* show with Matt Lauer, in which Cruise criticized psychiatry and prescription drugs.

Industry analysts say the leaked video reinforces the eccentric public persona Cruise has struggled to shake since 2005.

"This video was meant for an internal audience of believers, so to the average viewer, the jargon and the intensity come off as deeply bizarre," said Hollywood branding expert Howard Bragman. "When you pair that with a major biography claiming you essentially run a secretive religious organization, it creates a massive PR headache."

As of Thursday morning, the video continues to gather hundreds of thousands of views across various Web sites, while Morton's book has rapidly climbed to the top of the Amazon best-seller list. 

Representatives for Cruise did not immediately return CNN’s requests for further comment.
